Our method thus provides a universal computational tool for exploring the boundaries of quantum state space and the limits of quantum resources.

items.title: Magnetic Domains Stabilized by Symmetry-Protected Zero Modes
items.abstract: Understanding mechanisms for the breakdown of thermalization in closed quantum systems is a central problem in quantum many-body physics. We demonstrate strong nonergodic behavior in the XX model on coupled chains, where domain-wall initial states retain an inhomogeneous magnetization profile for arbitrarily long times. We find that this effect arises due to zero modes protected by chiral symmetry. Using an analysis based on the Lanczos algorithm, we identify evidence for a localization transition in the thermodynamic limit at a critical coupling between the chains. We further show that antiferromagnetic defects in the initial state and symmetry-breaking perturbations restore slow thermalization, whereas it remains robust for symmetry-conserving perturbations. These results establish that degenerate, symmetry-protected subspaces can give rise to thermodynamically stable nonergodic dynamics in experimentally accessible quantum systems.

items.title: Superextensive Charging Power in the Absence of Global Operations
items.abstract: Quantum batteries provide a setting to investigate whether quantum effects can enhance the rate of energy storage beyond classical limits. While superextensive charging power has been reported in a few models, the fundamental physical requirements for achieving such scaling remain unclear. Here we identify the growth with system size of the g -extensiveness of either the battery or charging Hamiltonian as a necessary condition for achieving superextensive charging power in direct-charging protocols. We prove that bounded g -extensiveness forbids superextensive power, irrespective of interaction order. This criterion also explains why many previously studied protocols fail to exhibit superextensive behavior despite involving interactions with large participation numbers. Crucially, we demonstrate that global operations are not necessary: superextensive power can be achieved using Hamiltonians of fixed interaction order that remain energy extensive, provided g -extensiveness grows with system size. We illustrate this mechanism using a modified central-spin model.

items.title: Distributed Quantum Simulation
items.abstract: Quantum simulation is a promising pathway toward practical quantum advantage by simulating large-scale quantum systems. In this Letter, we propose communication-efficient distributed quantum simulation protocols by exploring three quantum simulation algorithms, including the product formula, the truncated Taylor series, and quantum signal processing over a quantum network. Crucially, our protocols significantly reduce the local hardware requirements of individual quantum processing units while ensuring the overall gate complexity does not exceed that of standard monolithic architectures. Our protocols are further shown to be optimal by deriving a lower bound on the quantum communication complexity for distributed quantum simulations with respect to evolution time and the number of distributed quantum processing units. Additionally, our distributed techniques go beyond quantum simulation and are applied to distributed versions of Grover’s algorithm and quantum phase estimation. Our work not only paves the way for achieving a practical quantum advantage by scalable quantum simulation but also enlightens the design of more general distributed architectures across various physical systems for quantum computation.

items.title: Bayesian Phase Stabilization at the Shot-Noise Limit for Scalable Quantum Networks
items.abstract: High-precision optical phase stabilization in quantum networks is fundamentally constrained by the strict photon-flux and duty-cycle limits required to avoid disturbing fragile quantum states. This challenge becomes especially critical when coordinating multiple independent light sources for multistep quantum protocols. Here, we develop an integrated phase-stabilization framework that incorporates a Bayesian phase estimator to optimally extract information from sparse single-photon detection events. This approach outperforms conventional maximum-likelihood estimation and achieves the shot-noise limit under minimal photon flux. The framework enables real-time correction of combined phase noise from both nodal lasers and transmission fibers, facilitating a two-step excitation protocol for heralded entanglement generation between separate trapped-ion nodes via single-photon interference. Operating with a detected photon rate of ∼ 1 MHz and a duty cycle ≤ 6.5 % , the system maintains interferometric visibility > 97 % over fiber links of 10 km and 100 km. This phase control yields long-lived ion-ion entanglement with parity contrast exceeding 85%, enabling device-independent quantum key distribution with finite-size security analysis over 10 km and a positive asymptotic key-rate over 100 km. Moreover, the resulting memory-memory entanglement at 10 km survives beyond the average time required to establish it—a fundamental requirement for quantum repeaters. This Letter establishes a robust and scalable foundation for practical long-distance quantum networks.

items.title: Universal Closed Form for Dynamical Love Numbers of Black Holes
items.abstract: Black hole static Love numbers vanish, but their dynamical counterparts do not. We present the entire scheme-independent dynamical response F ¯ ℓ , s of a Schwarzschild black hole in closed form, to all orders in G , and for every spin s and multipole ℓ . The result is F ¯ ℓ , s / 4 π R S 2 ℓ + 1 = Φ ℓ , s ( y ¯ ) − 1 2 η Φ ℓ , s ′ ( y ¯ ) with y ¯ = − 1 2 η 2 τ and η = i ω R S . Here Φ ℓ , s is simply the leading-log solution to the renormalization group equation, but lifting the running logarithm to τ = log ( R S / R ) − 2 ∑ k ≥ 2 ζ k η k − 1 resums it to all orders. This tower of Riemann ζ values is the Newtonian phase in disguise: it originates from the long-range 1 / r potential in the far zone, and is universal across multipole and spin. Our result exhibits a factorization pinned to three ingredients: the strength of horizon absorption, the running rate in the near zone, and the dressed logarithm in the far zone. Using shell effective field theory, we independently verify our formula for scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational perturbations, reaching O ( G 15 ) .

items.title: Neutrino Emissivity in Δ -Direct-Urca Processes inside Neutron Stars
items.abstract: Observed massive neutron stars may contain heavier baryons such as Δ isobars and hyperons in their interiors. In the presence of Δ isobars, the neutrino emitting nucleonic Urca processes can be accompanied by Δ -direct-Urca processes involving nucleons and hyperons. Over the past three decades, significant theoretical effort has been dedicated to understanding the thermal evolution of neutron stars with the nucleonic and hyperonic Urca processes emerging as dominant cooling mechanisms. While recent studies have proposed the presence of Δ isobars in the dense core of neutron stars, the specific contribution of the Δ -direct-Urca process to neutrino emissivity has not been explicitly quantified. In this Letter, we address this gap by deriving the neutrino emissivity associated with Δ -direct-Urca processes in dense matter inside neutron stars. We show that once Δ -direct-Urca processes become kinematically allowed, their emissivities are comparable to those of nucleonic-direct-Urca processes.

items.title: Hidden Simplicity in AdS Spinning Mellin Amplitudes via Scaffolding
items.abstract: We uncover surprising hidden simplicity in Mellin amplitudes for tree-level anti–de Sitter (AdS) holographic correlators for AdS “gluon” (spin-1) operators. We define Mellin amplitudes with n spinning operators via the so-called scaffolding of 2 n -scalar ones with specific projection operators for each spin state, which are rational functions of Mellin variables of 2 n scalars generalizing flat-space scaffolding amplitudes. We classify possible three-point structures with spin 1, which take the same form as massive three-point amplitudes in flat space, and match them with special solutions such as those extracted from 6-scalar ones in AdS 5 × S 3 . Focusing on AdS 5 gluons, we directly bootstrap spinning amplitudes in scaffolding form up to n = 6 gluons (which amounts to 2 n = 12 scalars) using factorizations, multilinearity, and flat-space limit. The results take a remarkably simple form in analogy with flat-space amplitudes, which can be constructed from familiar 3- and 4-vertices as well as propagators of massive spin-1 particles. Surprisingly, we find that vertices with any descendant levels are proportional to the primary ones with nice combinatorial coefficients, which makes manifest the correct flat-space limit in the simplest possible way.

items.title: Geometry of In-In Correlators
items.abstract: We introduce a family of polytopes— in-in zonotopes —whose boundary structure organizes the contributions to scalar equal-time correlators in flat space computed via the in-in formalism. We provide explicit Minkowski sum and facet descriptions of these polytopes, and show that their boundaries factorize into products of graphical zonotopes and lower-dimensional in-in zonotopes, thereby mimicking the factorization structure of the correlators themselves. Evaluating their canonical forms at the origin—equivalently, calculating the volume of the dual polytope—reproduces the correlator. Finally, in a simple example, we show that the wave function decomposition of the correlator corresponds to a subdivision of the dual polytope.

items.title: Proton’s Isovector Parton Distribution Function with Updated Analysis of Large-Momentum Lattice Data
items.abstract: The proton’s unpolarized u ( x ) − d ( x ) parton distribution function (PDF) has been studied by a number of lattice QCD groups through large momentum expansion. However, due to lattice artifacts (excited state contaminations, unphysical pion masses, and discretization effects) and less-advanced theoretical analysis (renormalizations, large-distance extrapolations, and large-log resummations), the resulting PDFs cannot be compared strictly with experimental data. By using the state-of-the-art theoretical tools and mitigating the lattice artifacts empirically, we reanalyze the available datasets in the literature and find that the new PDF for the physical-limit-extrapolated dataset (MSULat20) is consistent with global fits within ∼ 1 σ , while others are broadly compatible. This provides evidence that large momentum expansion is capable of accurately predicting the x dependence of the PDFs when ideal lattice data become available.

items.title: Particle Correlations in Jets
items.abstract: We study particle correlations in high energy jets by comparing the measured energy-energy correlator with that constructed from two individual energy flows with respect to the jet axis. This comparison demonstrates that the genuine correlations are stronger at moderate or large angles across all jet energies, indicating that they are coming from correlated splitting. Meanwhile, at small angles, they increase with jet energy, exhibiting a peculiar pattern that can be used to explore jet energy loss in heavy-ion collisions. This method will provide a unique tool to disentangle different physics by comparing the genuine correlations in jet energy-energy correlators between heavy-ion collisions and proton-proton collisions.

items.title: Time-Dependent Wave-Packet Approach to Reactions for Quantum Computation
items.abstract: We describe a method for obtaining the scattering matrix for nuclear or chemical reactions on a finite lattice. Aside from the preparation of the initial and final states as wave packets, the only other operation required is unitary time evolution, making this approach ideal for simulations on quantum hardware. The central quantity is a time-dependent overlap between incoming and outgoing wave packets whose Fourier transform corresponds to the scattering matrix at fixed energy, from which one can calculate elastic and inelastic cross sections for reactions involving two interacting clusters. Working in Cartesian coordinates enables an efficient encoding of the problem on quantum hardware via the first quantization mapping, with favorable qubit scaling for describing asymptotic scattering states. Within this framework, we describe a quantum algorithm for probing the scattering amplitude through different angles, including the forward direction, which provides access to the total cross section via the optical theorem. We demonstrate our methods through a series of numerical examples, for both elastic and inelastic processes, comparing against exact calculations. The techniques we describe can more readily be extended to a large number of constituent particles than other existing approaches, once fault-tolerant quantum hardware becomes available.

items.title: Development and applications of an extended modified embedded-atom method interatomic potential for binary Ni-V alloys
items.abstract: Recent experiments show a binary Ni-V face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution alloy possessing superior strength and work hardenability exceeding extant multiprincipal element alloys with an FCC solid solution structure. The outstanding mechanical properties can be attributed to V solid solution strengthening, but the mechanistic effects of V solutes and short-range order (SRO) on deformation behavior remain unclear and perplexing. Here, we develop an extended modified embedded-atom method (XMEAM) interatomic potential for the binary Ni-V system to enable direct and accurate modeling of SRO and V-lattice defect interactions. The potential is fit to a broad range of lattice and defect properties from extant experiments and new density functional theory (DFT) calculations in multiple solid solution and intermetallic structures. Extensive benchmarks with molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations show great accuracy and transferability of the developed potential in Ni-V solid solution alloys across a wide range of V concentrations as well as in intermetallic structures. In particular, the potential reproduces SRO, phase transitions, solute misfit volume and solute interaction with dislocations consistent with extant experiments and the Ni-rich side of the binary phase diagram. The new potential is also computationally efficient; its availability thus opens the essential path for large-scale, mechanistic modeling of plastic deformation and SRO effects in the Ni-V binary system with high fidelity and forms the foundation for developing other binary systems and extending to ternary systems.

items.title: Atomic-scale phase-field modeling with many-body interactions
items.abstract: Based on free-energy functionals, phase-field modeling enables the simulation of microstructural pattern formation and dynamics while providing spatially resolved information on the underlying local thermodynamics. In the same spirit, free-energy functionals for atomic systems can be used for analogous purposes at atomic resolution; we refer to this approach as atomic-scale phase-field modeling. However, previous attempts have been limited to classical pairwise interatomic potentials because of the high computational cost and limited scalability associated with evaluating free-energy functionals involving many-body interactions. In this work, we generalize the atomic-scale phase-field methodology to many-body systems, whose efficient evaluation is facilitated by modifying the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (order- N SSCHA) and by machine-learning potentials. We apply this method to bulk Cu and Si in the NPT ensemble, where the predicted equilibrium lattice constants show agreement with molecular-dynamics simulations, validating the theoretical framework for these relatively simple systems. Furthermore, we apply the method to the Σ 5 ( 310 ) [ 001 ] grain boundary in Cu using a simulation cell containing several hundred atoms, yielding atomically resolved maps of local free-energy distributions. The results reveal a pronounced concentration of free energy at the grain-boundary core, suggesting a possible coupling between tensile stress and entropy. We then applied the developed methodology to more complex materials, namely, the thermal expansion of SrTiO 3 and the polarization-dependent free-energy surfaces of PbTiO 3 . For these systems, the agreement with other methods was less satisfactory than for the simpler benchmarks, revealing the current limitations of the framework and identifying directions for further development. This study represents a step toward the accurate free-energy functionals applicable to large-scale atomic systems, thereby advancing the atomic-scale phase-field concept.

items.title: Oxygen deficiency and valency reconstruction in multiferroic V-doped HfO 2
items.abstract: The interplay of oxygen deficiency and vanadium multiple valency in the candidate multiferroic V-doped P c a 2 1 hafnia HfO 2 is studied by first-principles calculations. Low-lying V majority gap states accept electrons from oxygen-vacancy donors, reducing their formation energy, and converting nominal V 4 + centers into V 3 + . The resulting local magnetization and screening changes are reflected in the calculated V core-level shifts, which are consistent with the experimentally observed x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy signatures. The calculated V 3 + / V 4 + population ratio determined by oxygen vacancies only matches experiment in reducing conditions, suggesting that additional electron reservoirs may contribute under atomic-layer-deposition growth conditions. A similar scenario also seems to apply to the recently observed multiferroicity in Cr-doped hafnia, where oxygen deficiency is expected from the synthesis route.

items.title: Recovering long-range cumulative response to geometric frustration in quasi-one-dimensional systems, mediated by constitutive softness
items.abstract: Cumulative geometric frustration can drive self-limited assembly and morphology selection through size-dependent energetic costs. However, the slenderness of quasi-one-dimensional systems generally suppresses the formation of long-range longitudinal gradients. We show that the suppression of longitudinal gradients can be overcome by tuning the ratio between the longitudinal and transverse (shear) moduli. We demonstrate the recovery of cumulative frustration across distinct quasi-one-dimensional systems, each frustrated through a different mechanism, by the introduction of a soft response mode. The resulting saturation length scale is universal and is dictated by the local constitutive information of the system.

items.title: Fully analytical description of the compositional trends in III-V ternary nanomaterials based on group V intermix
items.abstract: We present a fully analytical description for the stationary vapor-solid (VS) distributions of III-V ternary epilayers and nanomaterials of different types in the most complex case of ternaries with two highly volatile group V elements. The approach is based on the minimum free energy principle and a self-consistent determination of the total growth rate of a ternary structure. This enables one to circumvent the uncertainty in the unmeasurable concentrations of group V atoms in a mother phase. The analytic VS distribution is a combination of the kinetic Langmuir-McLean distribution and the equilibrium distribution, whose weights are regulated by the effective III/V ratio. The model fits well the whole set of data on the stationary compositions of epilayers and catalyst-free and vapor-liquid-solid nanowires in the four material systems AlS b x As 1 − x , InS b x As 1 − x , In P x As 1 − x and Ga P x As 1 − x and provides a method for controlling the compositions of III-V ternary nanomaterials by the growth parameter tuning.

items.title: Remote synchronization and critical-like breakdown in star networks of oscillator populations
items.abstract: Remote synchronization, in which indirectly connected nodes synchronize while the mediating hub remains desynchronized, is a counterintuitive form of collective dynamics in complex networks. Most previous studies have treated each node as a single oscillator, whereas nodes in realistic systems often represent populations of interacting dynamical units. Here, we study remote synchronization in a star network whose nodes are Kuramoto oscillator populations. Each node contains many internally coupled oscillators with coupling strength K , and different nodes interact through an internode coupling strength L . We show that remote synchronization emerges only at an intermediate level of internal synchrony: The leaf nodes become strongly synchronized with each other, while the hub remains weakly synchronized with them, when the internal order parameter is neither close to zero nor close to one. Increasing K further causes an abrupt breakdown of the remote-synchronized state. Detrended fluctuation analysis reveals enhanced scaling behavior and critical-like long-range temporal correlations near this breakdown boundary. A two-parameter scan in the ( L , K ) plane confirms that the remote-synchronized regime occupies a finite region associated with intermediate internal order and relatively low detrended fluctuation analysis exponent. We further provide a phenomenological effective-phase interpretation, showing that internal coupling controls the coherence, susceptibility, and stability of each oscillator population. These results demonstrate that internal population dynamics can regulate both the emergence and critical-like breakdown of remote synchronization.

items.title: SIETAS model: Swarm-informed triggering, earthquake diffusion, and multiscaling applied to the current Campi Flegrei unrest
items.abstract: Earthquake diffusion is commonly interpreted either as the migration of fluids or as the propagation of triggering cascades within branching processes. In the latter framework, anomalous diffusion emerges naturally from the long-memory kernels of epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) models. Here, we introduce a swarm-informed ETAS (SIETAS) model designed to describe volcanic seismic swarms. The model combines a temporally truncated power-law triggering kernel with a spatially localized logistic kernel, thereby introducing intrinsic temporal and spatial scales into the triggering process. Using an AI earthquake catalog from the ongoing Campi Flegrei unrest, we show that SIETAS provides a substantially better description of seismicity than the standard ETAS formulation. We further demonstrate that earthquake diffusion exhibits clear multiscaling behavior characterized by three effective scaling regimes. Analytical arguments based on branching-process theory and continuous-time random walks indicate that the SIETAS kernels generate a crossover from transient anomalous diffusion to an effectively normal-diffusive regime, followed by saturation due to finite subcriticality. We discuss how the observed multiscaling behavior may emerge from the interplay between short-time triggering, finite temporal memory, finite spatial localization, and secondary components of the triggering kernel. These results establish a connection between swarm-informed earthquake triggering and multiscale diffusion phenomena in volcanic environments.

items.title: Long-time exponential decompositions of non-Markovian Gaussian baths
items.abstract: Gaussian baths are widely used to model non-Markovian environments, yet the cost of accurate simulation at long times remains poorly understood, especially when spectral densities exhibit nonanalytic behavior as in a range of realistic models. We rigorously bound the complexity of representing bath correlation functions on a time interval [ 0 , T ] by sums of complex exponentials, as employed in recent variants of pseudomode and hierarchical equations of motion methods. These bounds make explicit the dependence on the maximal simulation time T , inverse temperature β , and the type and strength of singularities in an effective spectral density. For a broad class of spectral densities, the required number of exponentials is bounded independently of T , achieving time-uniform complexity. The T dependence emerges only as polylogarithmic factors for spectral densities with strong singularities, such as step discontinuities and inverse power-law divergences. The temperature dependence is mild for bosonic environments and disappears entirely for fermionic environments. Thus, the main bottleneck for long-time simulation is the presence of sharp nonanalytic features in the bath spectrum. Our results are instructive both for long-time simulation of non-Markovian open quantum systems and for Markovian embeddings of classical generalized Langevin equations with memory kernels.

items.title: Instability-enhanced quantum sensing with tunable multibody interactions
items.abstract: Dynamical instabilities can amplify small perturbations into measurable signals, offering a route to quantum-enhanced sensing. This mechanism was experimentally demonstrated in a collective spin system with quadratic interactions, described by a twist-and-turn Hamiltonian, where quantum evolution near an unstable point leads to exponential growth of spin fluctuations, enabling metrological gain beyond the standard quantum limit. Here, we show that a quartic extension of this Hamiltonian substantially increases the amplification. This additional nonlinear term reshapes the phase-space structure, generating new unstable fixed points with larger local Lyapunov exponents and therefore faster signal amplification at shorter evolution times. Remarkably, even for the same instability rate (equal Lyapunov exponent), collective multibody interactions outperform the quadratic case, demonstrating that metrological gain is not determined by the Lyapunov exponent alone. We show analytically that the finite-time growth of the gain is governed also by the local phase-space curvature around the unstable point. Only for a symmetric unstable point, as in the quadratic case, is the finite-time gain described by the Lyapunov exponent alone. Our results identify local phase-space curvature as an additional resource for optimizing the speed and performance of quantum sensors.

items.title: Efficient simulation of Bose-Einstein condensates in nontrivial topologies
items.abstract: Bubble-shaped Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) constitute a unique class of quantum fluids with a hollow, thin-shell geometry that supports a wide variety of phenomena distinct from those of compact condensates. Numerical simulation of such systems is particularly challenging due to their inherently three-dimensional structure and extreme aspect ratios. We present an efficient finite-difference simulation framework for solving partial differential equations in nontrivial topologies, with a focus on the static and dynamical modeling of bubble-shaped BECs. By employing selective spatial sampling on a semistructured grid, our method substantially reduces memory usage and achieves more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in computational performance compared with conventional split-step Fourier solvers. The algorithm is naturally extendable to highly parallel execution on graphics processing units (GPUs), enabling large-scale, time-dependent simulations of thin-shell condensates. We apply this framework to simulate the formation of bubble BECs through a controlled hollowing-out protocol using ab initio trapping potentials relevant to the Cold Atom Laboratory aboard the International Space Station. From these simulations, we identify characteristic timescales and parameter ramps required to achieve adiabatic evolution, thereby assessing the feasibility of experimentally realizing bubble-shaped condensates in microgravity environments.

items.title: High-fidelity molecular quantum logic gates resilient to interaction fluctuation
items.abstract: Optically trapped polar molecules are promising for quantum information processing, yet the accuracy of an entangling molecular gate is limited by the uncertainty of dipole-dipole interactions (DDI) from the molecular motion in traps. We show that two π pulses of global microwave excitation can yield a spin-echo controlled-phase gate when assisted by two single-qubit gates, where the gate is resilient to the uncertainty of DDI because it strongly suppresses populating DDI-coupled states. Further, the controlled phase is fully tunable by varying the relative phase of the two global microwave pulses, and, hence, is applicable in a wide range of quantum algorithms involving quantum Fourier transform. We introduce a motional-mode separation technique to quantum mechanically study the influence of the molecular motion, which shows that the motion-induced infidelity of the gate can be below 0.0001 with typical experimental conditions.

items.title: Ultraslow diffusion emerging from local symmetry breaking in quenched disorder
items.abstract: Many dynamical systems operate in disordered environments. In this Letter, we investigate how quenched randomness modifies particle diffusion. We show that, in finite-strength potential landscapes, low disorder densities can induce logarithmically ultraslow diffusion. The underlying mechanism originates from local symmetry breaking in particular potential configurations: Barrier-well structures form directional channels, causing particles to undergo hierarchical capture, escape, and recapture processes. A coarse-grained channel theory yields an approximate scaling prediction for the mean-square displacement. Counterintuitively, when the disorder density reaches the fully disordered limit, the system returns to normal diffusion, revealing a nontrivial, nonmonotonic relationship between disorder density and transport type. This mechanism is observed in both nonlinear maps and stochastic systems.

items.title: Pressure-induced unconventional charge-density-wave states in kagome metal AV 3 Sb 5 ( A = K , Rb, Cs)
items.abstract: Since the discovery of charge density wave (CDW) and superconductivity, kagome metal AV 3 Sb 5 ( A = K , Rb, Cs) provides a new platform for exploring novel many-body quantum phenomena. In CsV 3 Sb 5 , a stripelike CDW with commensurate wave vector q = 3 / 8 was observed under moderate pressures, which leads to a peculiar superconducting double-dome behavior in pressure-dependent phase diagram. Previous density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicate that the pressure-induced stripelike CDW is beyond conventional phonon softening scenario, suggesting a nontrivial role of electronic correlations. However, an in-depth understanding for the pressure-induced unconventional CDW remains elusive. Here, we performed pressure-dependent V 51 nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements on KV 3 Sb 5 and RbV 3 Sb 5 . Although the superconducting double-dome behavior is absent in pressurized KV 3 Sb 5 and RbV 3 Sb 5 , a pressure-induced CDW phase, ascribed to a possible incommensurate triple- Q CDW, is identified by NMR spectra in both materials, indicating that the pressure-induced unconventional CDW beyond DFT calculations is a common feature for kagome metal AV 3 Sb 5 . In contrast to the stripelike CDW, the pressure-induced incommensurate triple- Q CDW does not strongly suppress the superconducting temperature ( T c ) but coincides with an almost plateau behavior at intermediate pressure regime in the pressure-dependent superconducting phase diagram. Furthermore, by systematically analyzing the Korringa relation between Knight shift and nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate in AV 3 Sb 5 , Van Hove singularity-driven electronic fluctuations are revealed as an effective knob for the pressure-induced unconventional CDW. Finally, our present findings underscore the pressure-induced unconventional CDW as a novel correlated quantum state in kagome metal AV 3 Sb 5 .

items.title: Intrinsic Floquet generation and 1 / I quantum oscillations in a sliding charge-density wave
items.abstract: Recent experiments [ Phys. Rev. B 109 , 245123 (2024) ] revealed striking inverse-current ( 1 / I ) quantum oscillations in quasi-one-dimensional charge-density-wave (CDW) insulators and proposed an intrinsic Floquet sideband mechanism arising from the sliding condensate. Here, we develop the complete theoretical framework underlying this proposal. We provide an exact Floquet diagonalization of the uniformly sliding CDW problem, yielding split gap edges and a ladder of Floquet sidebands with explicit unitary transformation and spectral functions. Using this exact solution, we formulate weak-probe tunneling spectroscopy and demonstrate that the local Floquet spectrum naturally yields 1 / I oscillations as successive sideband edges cross a fixed contact chemical potential. The measured period fixes N eff ε ≃ 4.80 eV , where ε is the local contact-to-gap-edge offset. Combining this relation with the experimentally resolved low-temperature oscillations constrains the effective coherent channel count to be at most of order 10 3 , far below the geometric estimate N geom ∼ 3 × 10 4 , while ε = 10 meV gives the representative value N eff ≃ 480 . This reduced coherent scale is naturally realized by a spatially nonuniform percolating network, but does not require N eff independent end-to-end wires. Furthermore, using a segmented multiterminal model, we show that inelastic phase-slip dephasing near the contacts explains the experimentally observed suppression of oscillation visibility on outer voltage probes. Finally, we contrast the persistent-current-driven multiterminal geometry with a homogeneous voltage-biased two-terminal reference calculation. Our results establish a nonequilibrium transport framework for the observed 1 / I oscillations and identify an observability condition in which the Floquet spacing must exceed collective and quasiparticle broadening.

items.title: Emergent dilemma and periodic oscillation in behavioral epidemics with nonlinear feedback
items.abstract: Human behaviors, particularly nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), are dynamically coupled with epidemic spreading. However, most models assume a linear relationship between perceived risk and infection rates, failing to capture the nonlinear nature of real-world behavioral responses. Here, we propose a behavioral epidemic model by incorporating nonlinear feedback and social influence, and analytically derive its critical thresholds. Notably, once the infection rate exceeds a critical threshold, the fraction of NPI adopters abruptly drops to zero, in contrast to classic findings in linear models. This paradoxical decline indicates a social dilemma: While abandoning NPIs is individually optimal at high infection rates, it collectively triggers an explosive epidemic surge. Furthermore, as the intensity of social influence increases, the system undergoes a Hopf bifurcation leading to periodic oscillations, which reflects a vicious cycle of recurrent epidemic waves. Finally, we confirm the robustness of this NPI-abandonment dilemma in networked populations. Our work illustrates rich emergent dynamics, challenging traditional perspectives on behavioral epidemiology.

items.title: Super-Klein tunneling in two-dimensional Lorentzian-type barriers in graphene
items.abstract: We introduce a two-dimensional model of spin- 1 / 2 Dirac fermions in graphene subjected to a highly tunable electric field, which exhibits super-Klein tunneling. The electric field can be continuously interpolated between two limiting configurations: a uniform electrostatic Lorentzian barrier with translational invariance and a chain of well-separated electrostatic scatterers. We demonstrate that super-Klein tunneling arises naturally as a direct consequence of the intrinsic connection of the model to free-particle dynamics, a relation that is established through methods of supersymmetric quantum mechanics, which provide an elegant and analytically tractable framework. Besides the mentioned super-Klein tunneling, scale invariance of the model and invisibility of the potential for particles of specific energy are revealed, and possible routes toward experimental realization are discussed.

items.title: From coupled Z 3 Rabi models to the Z 3 Potts model
items.abstract: We study a Z 3 -symmetric Rabi model that describes a three-level system coupled to two bosonic modes. We derive a mapping of the two-mode Z 3 Rabi model onto a qubit-boson ring. This mapping allows us to formulate a realistic implementation of the Z 3 Rabi model based on superconducting qubits. It also provides context for the previously proposed optomechanical implementation of the Z 3 Rabi model. In addition, we propose a physical implementation of the Z 3 Potts model via a coupled chain of Z 3 Rabi models.

items.title: Population pumping of vibrational and rotational quantum states in the triatomic hydrogen ion observed by electron-beam-assisted high-resolution spectroscopy
items.abstract: We present a technique to observe the optical manipulation of individual quantum states of H 3 + ions stored inside a heavy-ion storage ring, where the excitation is detected by electron-beam-assisted action spectroscopy. The transitions addressed here are chosen to enable multicolor spectroscopy of states far above the energetic barrier, where this molecule—with a triangular ground state—can sample linear geometries. This region of the spectrum has so far been inaccessible due to extremely weak direct transition strengths from the ground vibrational level. Our experiments pave the way for spectroscopy of the simplest polyatomic molecule in a previously unexplored energetic territory, which would benchmark theoretical data crucial for the understanding of this fundamental molecular system. Our results also demonstrate laser pumping to vibrationally and rotationally excited states of H 3 + , gaining model-dependent access to their relative dissociative electron recombination rates.

items.title: Heisenberg-limited metrology from the quantum-quench dynamics of an anisotropic ferromagnet
items.abstract: The emerging field of quantum magnonics seeks to understand and harness the quantum properties of magnons—quantized collective spin excitations in magnets. Squeezed magnon states arise naturally as the equilibrium ground states of anisotropic ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, representing an important class of nonclassical magnon states. In this work, we show how a qubit-conditioned quantum quench of an anisotropic ferromagnet can be used for Heisenberg-limited parameter estimation based on measurements of the qubit only. In the presence of ground-state squeezing, the protocol yields information about the eigenmode frequency of the coupled magnon-qubit system, whereas no information is gained in the absence of such squeezing. The protocol therefore leverages genuine quantum correlations in the form of magnonic squeezing while simultaneously relying on the equilibrium character of this squeezing—a feature distinctive to magnetic systems.

items.title: Spin-qubit leapfrogging: Dynamics of shuttling electrons on top of another
items.abstract: Spin shuttling has crystalized as a powerful and promising tool for establishing intermediate-range connectivity in semiconductor spin-qubit devices. Although experimental demonstrations have performed exceptionally well on different materials platforms, the question of how to handle areas of low valley splitting in silicon during shuttling remains unresolved. In this work, we explore the possibility of utilizing the valley degree of freedom, particularly in regions of low valley splitting, to allow mobile spin qubits to be shuttled through an occupied stationary quantum dot, thereby leapfrogging over the stationary electron. This not only grants a more enriched mobility for shuttled electrons, as it opens new possible routing paths, but also enables the implementation of an entangling swap γ two-qubit gate operation in the process. Simulating this process for different sets of parameters, we demonstrate the feasibility of such an operation and offer a unique use case for otherwise precarious regions of a quantum processor chip and propose a possible extension to the set of possible operations for silicon spin-qubit devices.

items.title: Effective particle size as a control parameter for rough hard-particle fluids
items.abstract: We numerically investigate how particle surface roughness affects the static and dynamic properties of a hard-particle fluid across a wide range of densities, ρ . These simulations of a simple model of granular systems reveal that, although the amplitude and coverage of surface corrugation significantly influence the ρ dependence of system properties, the qualitative behavior of this dependence remains unchanged. These findings can be described quantitatively by introducing an effective particle size, which enables a direct mapping of the rough particle systems to equivalent hard-disk systems. Analytical calculations provide an explicit form of this mapping and allow us to predict the static and dynamic properties of rough particles using standard liquid-state theories for hard disks.

items.title: Non-Abelian Quantum Signal Processing: A Composite Pulse for Fast Analytic Control of Hybrid Oscillator-Qubit Processors
items.abstract: Quantum signal processing (QSP) transforms a unitary parametrized by a classical variable θ into one governed by a polynomial function f ( θ ) . Though quantum mechanics is linear, such highly nonlinear transformations arise naturally from the curvature of the qubit Bloch sphere. This capability underpins many quantum algorithms and enables robust control by decreasing sensitivity to errors in a control parameter, or quantum sensing by increasing sensitivity to variations one seeks to measure. Here, we extend QSP from classical, commuting control parameters to noncommuting quantum operators. We call this new multivariate class non-Abelian QSP . Rather than treating the noncommutativity of quantum control variables as a complication, non-Abelian QSP exploits their richer commutator algebra as a resource for efficient control. A natural setting is hybrid oscillator-qubit systems realized in superconducting and trapped-ion processors, where the control variables can be the noncommuting position and momentum of a quantum harmonic oscillator. We introduce the Gaussian-controlled rotation (GCR), a canonical instance of non-Abelian QSP that cancels the Gaussian quantum-fluctuation error of an oscillator-controlled qubit rotation, matching the robustness of classical composite pulses with a much shorter circuit and an order-of-magnitude lower error. GCR enables fully analytical circuits for preparing squeezed, cat, GKP, and Fock states with performance comparable to state-of-the-art numerically optimized protocols. Building on this primitive, we develop an analytical framework for universal control of GKP bosonic codes, in which logical readout doubles as piecewise gate teleportation, yielding the first high-fidelity, error-mitigated single- and two-qubit logical gates for finite-energy GKP that surpass prior schemes even in the noiseless regime. The same framework supplies midcircuit error detection and extends in closed form to arbitrary lattices, qudits, and multimode codes relevant to the superconducting-circuit experiments now demonstrating beyond-break-even GKP memory. We further apply these ideas to close a key gap in oscillator-assisted quantum phase estimation. Together, these results show that the non-Abelian structure of quantum control operators can provide a practical resource for robust and efficient quantum control, establishing non-Abelian QSP as both a new theoretical framework and an experimentally accessible control paradigm.

items.title: Nonsymmorphic Time-Reversal-Doubled Axion Insulators
items.abstract: The axion insulator exhibits a topological magnetoelectric effect characterized by an axion angle θ = π , while the time-reversal-doubled axion insulator ( T -DAXI) can be viewed as two copies of an axion insulator related by time-reversal symmetry. In this work, we show that a nonsymmorphic topological crystalline insulator with glide (or screw) symmetry can host the nonsymmorphic T -DAXI phase, diagnosed by the nontrivial hourglass (screw) invariant δ h = 1 ( δ s = 1 ). In this phase, the partial axion angles ( θ ± = π ) are quantized by the glide and/or screw symmetry, and the gapped surfaces realize half-quantized quantum spin Hall states. Furthermore, we show that nonsymmorphic T -DAXIs also exhibit the spin-magnetoelectric effect. Namely, an external magnetic field can induce a topological nonlocal spin polarization in real space. When the magnetic field is time periodic, this leads to an alternating spin current detectable in experiment. Using ab initio calculations, we demonstrate that mixed bismuth monohalides Bi 4 Br x I 4 − x realize the nonsymmorphic T -DAXI. Our findings not only reveal the symmetry-enforced T -DAXIs in nonsymmorphic topological crystalline insulators, but also demonstrate the spin-magnetoelectric effect as a detectable topological spin response in nonsymmorphic T -DAXIs.

items.title: Topological Phase Transitions and Their Thermodynamic Fate in Arbitrary- S Classical Pyrochlore Spin Ice
items.abstract: We develop a self-contained theoretical framework that classifies the topological phases and critical phenomena of classical pyrochlore magnets with arbitrary spin S , subject to competing exchange and single-ion anisotropies. We work first in the monopole-free (ice-rule) limit. In the small- w regime, where the single-ion term favors low spin amplitudes, dualities reveal a dichotomy: Integer spins exhibit a continuous 3D X Y deconfinement transition, whereas half-integer spins remain in a U(1) Coulomb liquid without any transition. In the large- w regime, where the local spin amplitudes are maximized ( | S z | = S ), the macroscopic flux is quantized to multiples of 2 S . By mapping the defect structure to topological loop gases, we prove that the compatibility between the physical ice rule and the modular Z 2 S flux conservation holds at the vertex level if and only if S ≤ 3 / 2 . For S = 3 / 2 , this maps the system to the three-state Potts model, whose symmetry-allowed cubic invariant drives a first-order transition. For S ≥ 2 , no mapping to a discrete clock model exists. Using a decomposition of the partition function, we show that the only processes sensitive to the discrete Z 2 S structure carry exponentially small statistical weight and correspond to irrelevant operators at the 3D X Y fixed point, so the deconfinement transition is of the 3D X Y type. Finally, incorporating thermal monopoles, we show that they act as a symmetry-breaking effective magnetic field that severs defect strings. Consequently, the continuous transitions are rounded into crossovers, whereas the first-order S = 3 / 2 transition is predicted to survive at finite temperatures, terminating at a critical end point. Classical Monte Carlo simulations for S up to 7 / 2 corroborate the predicted crossover behavior at the accessible temperatures; these temperatures lie above the estimated critical end point, so the predicted survival of the S = 3 / 2 first-order transition remains to be tested directly.

items.title: Electric-Field-Induced X-Ray Nonreciprocal Dichroism in Hematite
items.abstract: Hematite ( α − F e 2 O 3 ) is a prototypical room-temperature antiferromagnet whose time-reversal-odd magnetic structure has recently attracted renewed attention. While such magnetic symmetry can be characterized in terms of higher-order multipoles beyond the magnetic dipole, their manifestation in measurable physical phenomena has remained largely elusive. In this work, we investigate x-ray absorption near the Fe K -edge of hematite under an applied electric field, which explicitly breaks space-inversion symmetry. We observe an electric-field-induced x-ray nonreciprocal linear dichroism that reflects the time-reversal-odd nature of the magnetic order. A symmetry-resolved multipole analysis attributes this response to the electric-field-induced magnetic quadrupole and the magnetic toroidal octupole induced by the applied electric field. Furthermore, numerical simulations based on ab initio density functional theory reproduce the observed spectra, including their dependence on the antiferromagnetic domain and x-ray polarization. These results indicate that electric-field-modulated x-ray absorption measurements, combined with simulations, provide a framework for identifying the higher-order multipoles contributing to measurable physical responses in time-reversal-odd antiferromagnets, thereby facilitating the investigation of hidden symmetry properties in magnetic materials.

items.title: OmniCosmos : Transferring Particle Physics Knowledge Across the Cosmos
items.abstract: Foundation models build an effective representation of data that can be deployed on diverse downstream tasks. Previous research showed that the OmniLearned , a foundation model for collider physics, could significantly advance discovery potential across collider experiments. In this paper, we show that foundation models trained on collider data can transfer to cosmology. Specifically, we improve the prediction of cosmological parameters and halo and galaxy velocities in different datasets from CosmoBench . To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a collider physics model has been shown to generalize across scientific fields.

items.title: Sampling Weights at Intermediate Temperatures is Optimal for Training Large Language Protein Models
items.abstract: Using a statistical mechanics framework, we investigate the parameter space of transformer models trained on protein sequence data. We sample the loss landscape at varying temperatures using Langevin dynamics to characterize the low-loss manifold and to understand the mechanisms underlying transformers’ superior performance in protein structure prediction. We find that, at variance with networks not based on the attention mechanism, the lack of a first-order-like transition in the loss of the transformer produces a range of intermediate temperatures with good learning properties; this is true for both synthetic and natural protein sequences. We also show that the parameters of most layers are highly conserved at these temperatures if the dimension of the embedding is optimal, and we provide an operative way to find this dimension. Additionally, we show that the attention matrix is more predictive of the contact maps of the protein at higher temperatures and for higher dimensions of the embedding than those optimal for learning. Finally, we showed that the models sampled at intermediate temperatures can predict the free-energy variation upon mutation, better than models obtained through standard optimization techniques.

items.title: Mechanosensitive Remodeling Sustains Rigidity Homeostasis and Elastic Memory in Actin Cortex Models
items.abstract: The actin cortex is a dynamic biopolymer network that, despite constant architectural changes through the assembly and disassembly of filaments and crosslinkers, sustains a rigid homeostatic state, i.e., a steady state of positive elastic moduli, and exhibits an elastic memory that far outlasts the structural turnover timescale. We still lack simple models that maintain collective rigidity and elastic memory at long times compared to the turnover time. To address this, we develop two complementary elastic network models in which rigidity homeostasis and long-lived elastic memory with complete turnover emerge as a result of mechanosensitive dynamics of filaments (edges) and crosslinkers (nodes), respectively. Both models require the following minimal ingredients: (1) preferential disassembly of edges or nodes under small tension or force, (2) a small but nonzero rate of random disassembly, and (3) energy injection upon assembly. Our models are robust to variations in random disassembly rates, can recover from drastic structural disruption, and exhibit diffusion of nodes and edges in steady state, displaying representational drift similar to that found in neuronal activities and physical learning circuits. We propose that the cortex is an example of “tunable matter,” i.e., its mechanosensitive remodeling dynamics tune properties of its edges and nodes so that the cortex as a whole can maintain robust but flexible rigidity in fluctuating mechanical environments.

items.title: Λ -Enhanced Gray-Molasses Loading and EIT Cooling of Neutral Atoms in Nanophotonic Traps
items.abstract: Nanophotonic traps for cold atoms typically have trap volumes that are orders of magnitude smaller than, e.g., free-space optical tweezers. This makes efficient loading of these traps challenging, thereby limiting the total number of atoms coupled to the nanophotonic waveguide. Here, we demonstrate that Λ -enhanced gray-molasses ( Λ GM ) can substantially increase the number of trapped atoms in a nanofiber-based cold-atom setup. Specifically, we observe a sixfold increase in the number of loaded atoms compared to conventional red-detuned polarization-gradient cooling. Despite the unusually small depth of our optical trap of only 24 μ K , we load about 4000 individual cesium atoms, achieving optical depths exceeding 140 and reaching the collisional blockade regime over a length of approximately 1 mm. After loading, we perform efficient electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT)-assisted cooling that is found to increase the trap storage time to 400(9) ms. This is a fivefold improvement over the passive storage time. Remarkably, we observe that EIT-cooling also works with two co-propagating nanofiber-guided light fields and requires only a few hundred picowatts of optical power. Our results provide an efficient method to boost both the number of loaded atoms and the storage time of nanophotonic atom traps.

items.title: Predicting Magic from Very Few Measurements
items.abstract: The nonstabilizerness of quantum states is a necessary resource for universal quantum computation, yet its characterization is notoriously demanding. Quantifying nonstabilizerness typically requires an exponential number of measurements and a doubly exponential classical post-processing cost to evaluate its standard monotones. In this work, we show that nonstabilizerness is, to a large extent, in the eyes of the beholder: it can be witnessed and quantified using any set of m n -qubit Pauli measurements, provided the set contains anti-commuting pairs. We introduce a general framework that projects the stabilizer polytope onto the subspace defined by these observables and provide an algorithm that estimates magic from Pauli expectation values with runtime exponential in the number of measurements m and polynomial in the number of qubits n . By relating the problem to a stabilizer-restricted variant of the quantum marginal problem, we also prove that deciding membership in the corresponding reduced stabilizer polytope is NP-hard. In particular, unless P = NP , no algorithm polynomial in m can solve the problem in full generality, thus establishing fundamental complexity-theoretic limitations. Finally, we employ our framework to compute nonstabilizerness in different Hamiltonian ground states, demonstrating the practical performance of our method in regimes beyond the reach of existing techniques.

items.title: Fast Gates for Bit-Flip Protected Superconducting Qubits
items.abstract: Superconducting qubits offer an unprecedentedly high degree of flexibility in terms of circuit encoding and parameter choices. However, in designing the qubit parameters, one typically faces the conflicting goals of long coherence times and simple control capabilities. Both are determined by the wavefunction overlap of the qubit basis states and the corresponding matrix elements. Here, we address this problem by introducing a qubit architecture with real-time tunable bit-flip protection. In the first, the “heavy” regime, the energy relaxation time can be on the order of hours for fluxons located in two near-degenerate ground states, as recently demonstrated in Ref. [Hassani et al ., Nat. Commun. 14 (2023)]. The second, “light” regime, facilitates high-fidelity control on nanosecond timescales without the need for microwave signals. We propose two different tuning mechanisms of the qubit potential and show that base-band flux-pulses of around 10 ns are sufficient to realize a universal set of high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates. This realizes a hardware-efficient and strongly noise-biased qubit platform with analogies to cat qubits with the potential for efficient quantum error correction. We expect that the introduced concept of fast and real-time wavefunction control can also be applied to other hardware-protected qubit designs.

entries.title: Transport in multilayer graphene: resistance from stacking faults
entries.abstract: Multilayer graphene exhibits rich possibilities for stacking. While natural bulk graphite predominantly occurs in the Bernal structure, where layers are stacked in an $-ABAB-$ pattern, rhombohedral stacking has sprung to prominence recently. It is well known that Bernal graphite exhibits anisotropic transport, with high resistance to currents along the stacking axis. Careful experiments using pillar geometries have measured out-of-plane resistance, attributing it to stacking faults where planes slip out of the nominal $ABAB$ sequence. The observed resistance shows anomalously large, non-Gaussian, sample-to-sample variations. In this article, we build a theoretical framework to calculate $c$-axis resistance of graphene stacks with an arbitrary stacking arrangement. Our approach builds on the idea that, regardless of stacking sequence, we have in-plane translational symmetry. With in-plane momentum as a good quantum number, $c$-axis transport reduces to an effectively one-dimensional problem that can be addressed using the Landauer paradigm. We calculate the resistances of a variety of simple stacking faults in both Bernal and rhombohedral systems. We also calculate the resistance of a rhombohedral 'slab' embedded between Bernal leads. Remarkably, despite both Bernal and rhombohedral graphite being metallic, the system exhibits insulating behaviour. We attribute this to Fermi surface mismatch. We next calculate the resistance of a multilayer sample with stacking disorder. Resistance is non-self-averaging, akin to a one-dimensional wire where disorder has a strong localizing effect. The median resistance grows exponentially with stack size, indicating insulating character driven by localization. Our results demonstrate that transport measurements on mesoscopic graphitic pillars serve as signatures of stacking faults, and in particular, probe localization-driven physics.

entries.title: All-temperature superfluidity in two dimensions
entries.abstract: In local theories with short-range interactions, continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken in two spatial dimensions at nonzero temperature. $\mathrm{U}(1)$-symmetric models instead admit a Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) phase with quasi-long-range order and nonzero phase stiffness, which is normally destroyed at high temperatures by vortex proliferation. Here, we show that a BKT phase, and with it superfluidity, can persist to arbitrarily high temperatures. Using the large-$N$ expansion, we study a $(2+1)$-dimensional quantum field theory in which a complex scalar is coupled to the critical $\mathrm{O}(N)$ model. At the biconical fixed point, where the inter-sector coupling is negative, the thermal effective potential has a circle of minima with nonzero $\mathrm{U}(1)$ amplitude. Integrating out the gapped fluctuations yields an effective theory for the compact phase mode at distances large compared to $1/T$. Since temperature is the only scale at the fixed point, the phase stiffness grows linearly with temperature, with a proportionality factor that scales linearly with $N$ and is fixed entirely by the fixed point. This renders vortex operators irrelevant for sufficiently large $N$. We further show that the vortex fugacity is exponentially small in $N$.

entries.title: Long-lived local coherences at high temperature from frozen domain walls
entries.abstract: Local coherences between distinct charge sectors--measured by the single-particle Green's function or the transverse spin autocorrelation function--do not overlap with hydrodynamic modes. At finite temperature, therefore, they decay faster than any power law in generic chaotic systems. We present a mechanism by which these coherences can persist anomalously long, for integrable and chaotic spin chains (including the XXZ and Fredkin spin chains) that obey a quantum group symmetry. We show--using a Mazur bound derived from the quantum-group symmetry, together with locality and a "non-undershoot" assumption--that the transverse spin autocorrelation function $C(t) \equiv \langle \sigma^-_x(t) \sigma^+_x(0)\rangle$ can decay at most algebraically: $C(t) \gtrsim 1/t^2$. This bound is not tight: in the large-anisotropy limit of the XXZ spin chain, at infinite temperature, we explicitly compute $C(t) \sim \sqrt{3}/(18 \sqrt{t})$. We also compute this decay rate in the XXZ spin chain for general easy-axis anisotropy, and estimate it to scale as $C(t) \sim t^{-2/z}$ (for transport exponent $z$) in the chaotic models.

entries.title: Quantum oscillations in a solvable model of a Kondo insulator
entries.abstract: We study the effects of interactions on the low-energy density of states (SdH) and magnetization (dHvA) quantum oscillations (QOs) in a Kondo insulator. Toward this end we introduce a generalization of the periodic Anderson model with Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) interactions at each site that is exactly solvable in the large-$N$ limit, where $N$ is the number of flavors of the heavy $f$ electrons. We show analytically and numerically that the insulating state remains stable in terms of spectrum, thermodynamics, and transport at low temperatures even for interaction strengths much larger than non-interacting band gap of the hybridization-gap insulator. We analytically derive generalizations of Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) formulae, distinct for the SdH and dHvA QOs, for the interacting insulator. We find that the SdH oscillation frequencies, $F_0\pm \delta F$, corresponding to the conduction and valence band edges, can be weakly renormalized by interaction relative to their non-interacting values. In contrast, dHvA QO frequency $F_0$ is not renormalized by interactions, and remains the same as that for the non-interacting unhybridized bands. The QO amplitudes show a remarkable difference: the dHvA amplitude is essentially unaffected by interactions, while the SdH amplitude is strongly enhanced due to gap renormalization.

entries.title: Resonant enhancement of Raman scattering in a MoS$_2$ nanotube
entries.abstract: The whispering-gallery modes confined in the wall of a multiwall MoS$_2$ nanotube resonantly enhance the spontaneous Raman scattering by its own optical phonons. Near the A exciton the excitonic dispersion compresses the ladder and sweeps its spacing through all intralayer phonon energies of MoS$_2$, so the match, reached for $A_{1g}$ at $E_{\rm pump}=1551$~meV, requires no geometric tuning. A missed match splits the excitation peak into a pump- and a scattered-resonant doublet whose splitting measures the residual detuning. Selection rules confine the double resonance to the TM$\to$TM channel and exclude $E_{1g}$.

entries.title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
entries.abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

entries.title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
entries.abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.

entries.title: Identifying intercalation electrodes for electrochemical ion recovery and desalination
entries.abstract: Water sources serve as a requirement for human consumption, industrial, and agricultural needs and a resource for valuable ions. Appropriate treatment of water that captures ions from the aqueous solution can give rise to suitable `products', such as critical ions (such as Li$^+$) in selective ion recovery and usable water in the case of desalination (i.e., removal of non-essential ions). Among myriad ion capture techniques, we focus on electrochemical methods using intercalation electrodes, an energy-efficient approach capable of both selectively extracting specific ions or non-selectively extracting multiple ions from diverse water sources. However, practical realization of electrochemical ion capture requires the use of robust cation intercalation electrodes, with the state-of-the-art olivine-FePO$_4$ and spinel-Mn$_2$O$_4$ exhibiting several shortcomings. Thus, we develop a high-throughput computational workflow to identify potential intercalation electrodes for both ion recovery and desalination from a pool of 20,414 Li, Mg, Ca, Na, and/or K-containing structures from the Materials Project database. Based on the construction of Pourbaix diagrams relevant for electrodes operating under seawater conditions, modifying criteria used for defining metastability in seawater, computing average intercalation voltages and the extent of metastability of electrode structures, and computational graphs to encode ionic selectivity, we identify a total of 11 promising electrodes for selective ion recovery and one possible desalination electrode. The promising materials identified in this work include Fe$_2$(MoO$_4$)$_3$, Li$_3$Fe$_2$(PO$_4$)$_3$, LiFeP$_2$O$_7$ for selective Li-recovery. Our study provides thermodynamic insights, qualitative trends, and a promising list of intercalation electrodes for experimental testing that should advance the field of electrochemical ion recovery.

entries.title: Transition-Metal-Oxygen Covalency Controls Ligand-Hole Stability in Li-Rich Cathode
entries.abstract: Lithium-rich cathodes boast a large specific capacity due to the presence of excess lithium per transition metal. However, making use of that excess Li drives the cathodes to unusually high formal oxidation states, often triggering unwanted side reactions, typically signaled by gas release and commonly associated with oxygen oxidation. By varying the transition metal (TM) chemistry in Li-rich materials, cyclability can vary drastically, with some materials suffering rapid capacity fade while others are able to maintain large and stable voltage windows. Such observations indicate a crucial role for both TM and O activities, but the details remain elusive. Here, we model core-level spectroscopy to understand differences in the charge compensation mechanism between different Li2MO3 (M = Mn, Ru, Ir) cathode materials. We find that ligand holes are important throughout the series, but their stability depends strongly on the transition-metal-oxygen electronic structure. In Li2MnO3, the ground state is already strongly negative-charge-transfer-like, so further delithiation rapidly increases ligand-hole character and promotes instability. Moving from Mn to Ru and Ir increases TM-O hybridization while reducing the tendency toward an extreme negative-charge-transfer state, allowing additional holes to remain delocalized over the covalent TM-O network over a wider range of charge. These results identify TM-O covalency, rather than the absence of oxygen-hole character, as a key factor controlling reversible high-valent redox and suggest a route for stabilizing high-energy-density cathodes without invoking reversible molecular oxygen formation.

entries.title: Material dependence of direct light-induced charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbates
entries.abstract: Direct injection of charge from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbed molecules via the chemical interface damping of localized surface plasmons has emerged as a promising avenue to avoid the rapid thermalization of hot carriers. The largest electron injection rates in the optical photon ranges are obtained for Al, Ag, Cu and Au, with Cu and Au showing significant plasmonic enhancement. The non-plasmonic metals show weak electron injection as a consequence of their high LUMO energies relative to the metal Fermi level. The results of our study pave the way towards a rational design of metallic nanoscale photocatalysts for specific chemical processes.

entries.title: Casimir Sign Reversal from Finite-Range Bogoliubov Fluctuations

We further discuss how the resulting nonlinear force law could be probed through the frequency response of a driven nanomechanical resonator.

entries.title: One-way electron mirrors from single-layer stacking shifts in rhombohedral graphite

Because stacking solitons glide under external fields, this mirror forms a movable element of electron optics defined by the crystal structure alone.

entries.title: Localized states of the non-Hermitian Schr{ö}dinger equation with a complex $1/r^{2}$ potential: from Efimov states to bipolarons
entries.abstract: We study the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation with a complex $1/r^{2}$ potential, which bridges Hermitian few-body and non-Hermitian many-body physics: a real attractive potential describes Efimov bound states, whereas a purely imaginary one describes the medium-induced interaction between two heavy polarons at large separations. We solve this equation analytically, obtaining both the localized and continuum states, and compare the solutions with numerical and WKB results. As the imaginary part of the potential is increased, the energies of the Efimov bound states acquire imaginary parts and rotate counterclockwise in the complex plane. On approaching the purely imaginary potential, the excited states disappear sequentially, while the Efimov ground state is smoothly connected to a bipolaron state localized at short distance. Such a bipolaron is localized solely by the medium-induced imaginary interaction, without any attractive real potential. Solving the equation by finite differences, we find that each bipolaron state is necessarily accompanied by another localized state that oscillates on the scale of the mesh size and hence has no counterpart in the continuum limit. Each such pair coalesces at an exceptional point as the strength of the purely imaginary potential is varied, whereas the coalescence is lifted once a finite real part is introduced. We show that this behavior originates from a symmetry of the discretized Schrödinger equation that holds for any purely imaginary potential.

entries.title: Strain-enhanced superconductivity in RuO$_2$ thin films: Joint experimental and theoretical studies

entries.title: Plasmon Collapse in a Directional Strange Metal
entries.abstract: Strange metals are widespread in strongly correlated quantum matter and closely intertwined with high-temperature superconductivity and quantum criticality, yet their microscopic charge dynamics remain fundamentally unresolved. Whether well-defined collective modes survive in an incoherent electronic fluid or dissolve into overdamped continua remains intensely debated. Here, employing high-momentum-resolution inelastic electron scattering complemented by direction-resolved transport, we show that the van der Waals compound $\mathrm{MoOCl}_2$, a "bad" metal known to host unusually "good" plasmons, exhibits a striking dichotomy in electronic coherence and charge dynamics. Transport reveals coherent Fermi liquid behavior along one in-plane crystallographic axis and an incoherent strange metal response along the orthogonal axis. This dichotomy extends directly to the charge response. The Fermi liquid direction supports a well-defined, long-lived plasmon, whereas the strange metal direction exhibits an overdamped excitation that progressively loses its collective character with increasing momentum. Beyond a critical momentum ($q_c$ $\approx$ 0.008 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$), the mode undergoes a reversal into negative dispersion and ultimately collapses into a broad, nearly featureless continuum with a robust high-energy boundary ($E_c$ $\approx$ 1.75 eV). Remarkably, thickness-dependent measurements show that both $q_c$ and $E_c$ remain nearly unchanged despite substantial modifications of Coulomb screening, revealing them as intrinsic scales of incoherent charge density fluctuations. These results establish a unique single-material platform in which coherent and incoherent electronic states are partitioned into in-plane orthogonal channels, and demonstrate that incoherent electronic fluids retain intrinsically structured charge dynamics beyond the quasiparticle paradigm.

entries.title: Dynamical phase transition for a logarithm observable in chaotic systems
entries.abstract: We consider the full distribution $P_N(A)$ of the dynamical observable $A = - \sum_{i=1}^N \ln x_i$ where $x_1, \dots, x_N$ is a sequence generated by a chaotic map $f(x)$ via $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$. We study the particular cases where $f(x)$ is the doubling, tent or logistic map, and focus on the limit $N \gg 1$. Typical fluctuations of $A$ are Gaussian with mean $\left\langle A\right\rangle$ and variance which are both of order $\sim N$. We find that the left tail of the distribution ($A < \left\langle A\right\rangle$) scales as $P_{N}(A) \sim e^{-NI(A/N)}$, and calculate the rate function $I(a)$ which depends on the map $f(x)$. Interestingly, we find that the right tail of the distribution ($A > \left\langle A\right\rangle$) follows an anomalous scaling: $P_{N}(A) \sim e^{-N^{1/3} F((A-\left\langle A\right\rangle) / N^{2/3})}$. The large-deviation function $F(y)$ has a universal form for the three maps, differing only in the scaling constants. At a critical value $y=y_c$, it exhibits a corner singularity which has the character of a condensation transition. The transition separates between a subcritical phase $0< y<y_c$ in which the fluctuations are Gaussian and arise homogeneously from all of the $x_i$'s, and a supercritical phase $y>y_c$ in which a small fraction of the $x_i$'s give a macroscopic contribution to the fluctuation. Despite this anomalous behavior of the right tail, we find that the cumulants of the distribution $P_N(A)$ grow linearly with $N$ at large $N$, and calculate the associated coefficients.

entries.title: Transdimensional Chern insulators in rhombohedral multilayer graphene superlattices

entries.title: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap: Solving fractional quantum Hall ground states
entries.abstract: Strongly interacting ground states are usually computed in finite systems and then extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit (TDL). For Laughlin and Pfaffian parent Hamiltonians, it reproduces exact pair-correlation functions and low-lying orbital entanglement spectrum (OES) nearly level by level. For Coulomb interactions, the rigorous TDL energy bounds closely match thermodynamic estimates from exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extrapolations, and the local diagnostics recover established Laughlin and Moore--Read OES counting and Friedel oscillations of the composite Fermi liquid. Beyond these benchmarks, the bootstrap resolves the thermodynamic ground states at $\nu=1/4$ and $\nu=12/5$, identifying a composite Fermi liquid and $\overline{\mathrm{RR}}_3$ topological order, respectively. The same framework applies equally well to Abelian and non-Abelian, gapped and gapless quantum Hall states. The TDL bootstrap therefore provides a general ground-state solver that determines both the energy and the state directly in the TDL.
